item.title: Attribution Is Not Resolution: AI Diagnosis, Organizational Context, and a Low-Cost Bypass
item.description:
This is a retrospective of a real incident-handling process. Names, the company, the platform, and locations are all anonymized; only two numbers are kept—the number of steps in the checklist and the time to closure—because the judgments below rest on them.

The conclusion first: in the diagnosis phase of this incident, the best performer was AI—one question narrowed the candidate causes down to the right category. Human troubleshooting had reached the same conclusion months earlier, yet stopped right there once the attribution was done. What actually pushed the issue to closure were two things AI could not do: knowing what the company itself had, and going on-site to pin down the mechanism that “verification happens only at PC login.” Attribution is not resolution—the breakpoint sits between root cause and workaround, and the input to that stretch is not reasoning power but organizational context.

item.title: What AI Cannot Replace: Customer-Facing Core Business Processes and the Engine That Runs Them
item.description: This post lays out a question I have been chewing on for a while: with AI this capable, what work can it not take over? My answer keeps converging on one place: customer-facing core business processes, and the process engine that carries them. This answer is not derived from first principles — it grew out of our work rebuilding our operations system, grinding through node after node of configuration. So I present it as “what we believe,” not “what must be” — if anything is off, push back.

item.title: Enterprise AI Adoption: Organizational Context, Internal FDEs, and Scenario Gates
item.description:
This post distills the framework we developed while building enterprise AI adoption plans: a four-level evolution path, four types of enterprise context, internal FDEs, three scenario gates, a five-stage rollout, and four governance pillars. Most AI projects stall at the pilot stage because nobody owns the organization, the data, and the processes—not because of the technology.

Over the past two years, companies have bought AI in nearly identical ways: purchase a batch of seats, run a few training sessions, pick two departments to pilot, then wait for the reports. Six months later, most of them are stuck at “individuals know how to use it,” while organizational capability hasn’t moved an inch.
